name: iOS
summary: Proprietary mobile operating system developed by Apple Inc. for the iPhone, resting on the hybrid Darwin/XNU kernel, the APFS file system and an integrated hardware security architecture.
license: Proprietary commercial (with low-level components released under the APSL and BSD licences)

content.introduction: iOS is the proprietary mobile operating system developed by Apple Inc. for its range of iPhone smartphones (and historically the iPod touch). Unveiled in 2007 under the initial name iPhone OS at the presentation of the first iPhone, it was renamed iOS in 2010. It is the technological and economic pillar of Apple's hardware and software ecosystem, transparently interconnected with the manufacturer's other platforms (macOS, iPadOS, watchOS, tvOS) through iCloud services, the synchronised keychain and continuity features.
content.what_is_it: Technically, iOS is a Unix-type operating system derived from macOS and built on the Darwin foundation. Its kernel is the hybrid XNU kernel (X is Not Unix), which combines the Mach 3.0 microkernel (for managing threads, tasks, virtual memory and inter-process communication through Mach ports) with a layer of BSD subsystems (for the POSIX process model, signal, user and TCP/IP network stack management) as well as the I/O Kit and DriverKit device driver frameworks. The upper user space, including the SpringBoard touch surface manager, is entirely proprietary.
content.origine_iphone_os_and_ios_naming: On 9 January 2007, Apple presented the iPhone at the Macworld Conference & Expo in San Francisco as a device combining a phone, a touch-controlled iPod player and an Internet communication terminal, equipped with a multi-touch interface. The press release announces availability in the United States in June 2007, in Europe at the end of 2007 and in Asia in 2008, with 4 GB and 8 GB models, and documents the supported radios: quad-band GSM, EDGE, 802.11b/g Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 2.0 EDR. The press release of 7 June 2010 presenting the iPhone 4 designates the system under the name iOS, in version 4, and mentions multitasking, folders and 1,500 new programming interfaces; the device is announced there for 24 June 2010 in the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Japan. These two press releases document the initial presentation and the use of the iOS name; they state no support period for the models.
content.frameworks_runtime_and_graphics: The iOS software environment rests on a four-layer architecture: Core OS, Core Services, Media and Cocoa Touch. Modern application development is carried out mainly in the Swift language (with support for the historical Objective-C runtime). Touch interfaces make use of the historical UIKit library and the modern declarative SwiftUI framework. 2D/3D graphical rendering and parallel computing are supported by the low-level Metal API, designed to minimise processor overhead. On-device artificial intelligence processing relies on CoreML, taking advantage of the hardware neural accelerators (Neural Engine) integrated into Apple Silicon chips.
content.home_screen_and_interface_gestures: The iOS interface is described in the iPhone user guide. On models equipped with Face ID, a swipe up from the bottom edge of the screen returns to the home screen; the same gesture followed by a pause opens the application switcher, and a swipe to the right or left moves from one open application to another. A swipe from the top right corner opens Control Centre, where a long press on a control reveals additional options and where the list of controls is modified in Settings > Control Centre. A double-click on the side button displays the default Apple Pay card and a triple-click activates the accessibility shortcut. Applications open from the pages of the home screen or from the App Library, reached by swiping left beyond the last page; this library, documented from iOS 14, automatically sorts applications by category, reorders the most used ones and places newly installed applications there. Apple also documents the customisation of home screen icons and widgets.
content.hardware_security_architecture_and_sandb: iOS security relies on close vertical integration between the silicon and the operating system. The boot sequence follows a hardware chain of trust (Secure Boot Chain) anchored in a root of trust in read-only memory (Boot ROM). An isolated cryptographic coprocessor, the Secure Enclave (SEP), handles biometric authentication (Face ID, Touch ID) and drives the hardware AES engine of the Data Protection system, encrypting each file individually. Every third-party application runs in a strict sandbox (App Sandbox) limiting its access to its own container directory, and any binary execution requires a valid cryptographic signature verified by the kernel at run time.
content.filesystem_storage_and_app_distribution: Since iOS 10.3, storage rests on the APFS file system (Apple File System), offering space sharing between volumes, instant file cloning and snapshot management. The system volume is mounted read-only in the form of a sealed volume signed cryptographically (SSV - Signed System Volume), ensuring the absolute integrity of the operating files during OTA software updates. Application distribution has historically taken place through the official App Store with prior review. In the European Union, in application of the Digital Markets Act (DMA), iOS includes support for alternative third-party application stores and for certified web distribution under notarisation control.
content.app_store_and_beta_testing_channels: Application distribution on iOS relies on the App Store, which Apple's developer documentation presents as a distribution channel to the devices of its platforms. Apple's deployment guide lists other methods: custom applications, unlisted applications, internal enterprise applications, and TestFlight for beta versions. TestFlight allows up to 100 members of the development team to be designated as internal testers, up to 10,000 external testers to be invited and up to 100 builds to be shared; the beta application description and review information are required for external testers. These distribution methods are distinct from the App Store's general public channel.
content.hardware_compatibility_and_ecosystem_sco: iOS is compiled exclusively for the 64-bit ARM64 architecture and runs only on chips designed by Apple (from devices with the A13 chip, such as the iPhone 11 and the second-generation iPhone SE). Apple provides a software support cycle of notable longevity for mobile devices, generally offering five to seven years of major system updates for each iPhone generation. The system cannot be installed on third-party non-Apple hardware and does not allow direct access to root administrative privileges for users in the standard configuration.
content.versions_and_device_support: The version presented by Apple on apple.com/ios is iOS 27. The published compatibility list covers the iPhone 11 and later models (Pro, Pro Max, mini), the second-generation iPhone SE and later, as well as the models announced since (iPhone 16e, 17e, Air, 18 Pro Max). The iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, equipped with the A12 chip, no longer appear there: support starts with devices with the A13 chip.
content.software_installation_update_and_downgra: Apple documents two iOS update paths. From the device, the update is performed in Settings > General > Software Update, after a backup and connection to a power source and a Wi-Fi network; if it does not appear, Apple describes updating from a computer: Finder on macOS Catalina or later, and a separate procedure for macOS Mojave or earlier and for Windows. Apple's security releases page states, as of 19 October 2026, that the latest iOS version is 27.0.1, published on 28 September 2026, that version 26.7.1 appears in the list on the same date and that version 27 is dated 14 September 2026; it states that after installing an update, iOS cannot be downgraded to the previous version. These pages set no period during which a given model receives updates.
content.apple_intelligence_requirements: Apple states that the current generation of Apple Intelligence works under iOS 27 on the iPhone 16 and later models, the iPhone 15 Pro, the iPhone 15 Pro Max and the iPhone Air. It requires that the device language and the Siri language be identical and appear among the supported languages, including French. The free space required reaches up to 14 GB on the iPhone 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max and Air, and up to 8 GB on the other compatible models. Siri AI is distributed as a beta. These conditions are additional to compatibility with iOS 27.
content.differences_with_ipados: iOS and iPadOS share the Darwin foundation and the XNU kernel, but Apple publishes two separate pages of new features and two separate lists of compatible devices since the formal separation of the two systems in 2019. iPadOS documents windowed multitasking, the Apple Pencil and pointing devices; the iOS page documents the features specific to the iPhone, including Apple Intelligence settings and accessories. A same version number therefore does not guarantee an identical set of features on the two systems.
content.documentation_and_resources: Apple publishes on apple.com/ios the new features of the current version and the list of compatible devices, and devotes a support article to the Apple Intelligence prerequisites. The pages refer to a separate developer area for frameworks and tools. Version and compatibility information changes with each annual cycle; no public commitment sets the support period of a given model.
advantages: State-of-the-art hardware security and encryption architecture (Secure Enclave, sealed APFS, strict sandbox).
Exceptional hardware and software optimisation ensuring great responsiveness and high energy efficiency.
Rich application ecosystem with high-performance modern frameworks (SwiftUI, Metal, CoreML).
Longevity of software support ensuring regular security and feature updates over several years.
Transparent integration and continuous synchronisation with all the devices of the Apple ecosystem.
Low-level components of the Darwin/XNU foundation published as open source on Apple's portal.
disadvantages: Commercial operating system, proprietary and closed in its application and graphical layers.
Strictly locked hardware ecosystem: runs exclusively on Apple iPhone smartphones.
Application distribution model controlled by Apple (despite a partial regulatory opening in the EU).
No access to root administrative privileges and strict restriction of low-level system customisation.
Impossibility of running or virtualising the system legally on hardware architectures not designed by Apple.
who_is_it_for: Smartphone users looking for a smooth, secure and intuitive daily user experience.
People invested in the Apple ecosystem making use of multi-device synchronisation (Mac, iPad, Apple Watch).
Professionals and enterprises requiring on-device data encryption and centralised MDM management.
Mobile developers targeting a highly monetised application market through Swift and Xcode.
who_is_it_not_for: Users requiring a fully free and open-source operating system, auditable end to end.
Computing enthusiasts wanting full access to root privileges and free modification of system components.
Consumers looking for entry-level devices or wishing to choose their hardware manufacturer freely.
Users refusing Apple's platform and App Store control policies.
content.verdict: iOS is Apple's mainstream mobile operating system. Through its vertical integration between Apple Silicon and the Darwin/XNU kernel, it combines hardware security and an application ecosystem managed by Apple, in a closed commercial environment controlled by its manufacturer.

relations.name: iPadOS
relations.note: Operating system dedicated to iPad tablets, historically derived from iOS and sharing the same Darwin/XNU foundation.

relations.name: Apple macOS
relations.note: Operating system for Mac computers sharing the Darwin/XNU kernel, the Swift frameworks and the Apple services ecosystem.
